definition: Strident means loud and harsh at once, with a scraping edge that is impossible to tune out.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word strident. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know strident should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The subway's brakes greeted every stop with a strident shriek that made tourists wince.
Loud is milder than strident — volume alone, with no edge to it.
Ear-splitting is louder and harsher than strident: strident scrapes at your patience, while ear-splitting simply overwhelms it.

Shrill is all about pitch — a sound piercingly high and hard on the ears, whatever its volume or texture. Strident is the fuller assault: loud, harsh, and grating at once, and always said with disapproval. A referee's whistle is shrill; a loudspeaker that is loud and rasping at once is strident.

Grating is about texture alone — a sound that rasps against the nerves like a file, even at low volume. Strident needs loudness as well: the harsh, loud, grating whole, disapproval included. A dry hinge merely grates; an old intercom at full cry is strident.

Latin stridere kept its screeching to itself: apart from stridor, a term doctors use for a harsh breathing sound, it produced no common English relatives. Strident carries the screech alone.

Strident is sound with an abrasive edge — loud, harsh, and impossible to tune out.
A voice, an alarm, or a tone of argument can all be strident; the word always carries disapproval, which separates it from merely loud, and its grating texture from shrill, which is only about pitch.
Strident condemns a sound — or a tone of argument — as loud and grating at once.
Shrill fixes on pitch, grating on texture, strident on the whole assault.
It pairs naturally with voices, alarms, and rhetoric; nothing gentle is ever strident.

For twenty years the ice-cream truck's jingle had been part of Maple Street's summers, and nobody had ever complained.
Then the speaker began to fail.
What had been a tinny but cheerful tune became strident: blared at full volume through a torn cone, every note arrived with a metallic rasp that carried three blocks.
Residents who once waved now winced.
A retired music teacher wrote to the county that the truck was 'an assault in waltz time,' and a petition gathered ninety signatures in a weekend.
The driver, baffled, pointed out that the tune itself hadn't changed -- same notes, same tempo, same route.
He was right, and it didn't matter.
The problem was never the melody; it was the harsh, deafening delivery.
A new speaker cost him eighty dollars and ended the war overnight.
